name: Electropoise

card.summary: A 1890s-1900s device sold as a body-wellness instrument that, worn against the skin, was claimed to improve circulation and vitality, an early example of appearance-and-health gadgets marketed to the public.
card.note: Historical device; physicians and courts challenged its claims.

quick.overview:
The Electropoise was a small metal device patented in the United States in 1897 by Hercules Sanche and marketed by the company Electrolibration. Advertising described it as a thermal instrument that, attached to the wrist or ankle and connected to cold water, would improve circulation, digestion and oxygen absorption and boost vitality.

Its connection to looks is through the era's wellness marketing, which tied vigor and a healthy complexion to such devices. Physicians of the time examined it critically, and a court case commented on the inventor's theory.
quick.how: Per period descriptions, a 'polarizer' was placed in cold water or on ice while a plate was attached to the wrist, ankle or another body part, with body warmth supposedly activating it.
quick.risks: Reported harms are mainly financial and the possibility of relying on it instead of medical care. Its claims were challenged in medical journals in 1897, 1913, 1915 and 1930, and the maker of a related device was jailed in 1915 for false curative claims.

lead: The Electropoise was a device patented in the United States by Hercules Sanche (US 588483, published August 17, 1897) and sold by Electrolibration, whose president John N. Webb said he was not a man of science [1]. It sold for about $25, in a range of $10 to $30 for similar devices such as the Oxydonor [1].
Advertising claimed it improved circulation, digestion and oxygen absorption, boosted vitality and purified the blood, though Sanche was said not to claim cures for diseases such as tuberculosis [1].

Physicians criticized it: a critical letter appeared in the Journal of the American Medical Association in 1897, with more critiques in 1913, 1915 and 1930. One physician, N.C. Morse, had a unit sawed open and reported nothing inside [1].

chain: Device worn against skin and linked to cold water
Claimed better circulation and oxygen uptake
angle.text: Marketers framed it as a way to improve circulation and vitality, the sort of general wellness promise period consumers associated with a healthier look. No appearance outcome has been documented.

paras: Sanche's device was marketed from Birmingham, Alabama, with offices in New York and London [1]. Sanche sued over a rival device, the Oxygenor; the court found insufficient evidence for the invention's value and ruled it could not be protected, calling his theory of 'diaduction' a pretense for obtaining a patent [1]. In 1915 E.L. Moses, inventor of a different device (the Oxypathor), was jailed for 18 months for false curative claims [1].
Critics argued that testimonials relied on post hoc reasoning, and one physician suggested the high price may have produced a placebo effect [1].

timeline.event: US patent 588483 published; critical letter appears in JAMA [1].
Maker of the Oxypathor jailed for false claims [1].
